**The quiet miracle of ordinary light.**

Most of the photons that have ever existed in the observable universe were created in the first few minutes after the Big Bang. They’ve been traveling ever since, redshifting into the cosmic microwave background—a faint, nearly uniform glow at about 2.725 kelvin that bathes everything. We don’t notice it with our eyes, but radio telescopes do. It’s the oldest light we can still see, a baby picture of the cosmos taken when the universe was only 380,000 years old.

That same light, stretched and cooled, now fills every cubic centimeter of space. On a clear night you can stand outside and know that some of those ancient photons are passing through your body right now. They’ve been on a 13.8-billion-year journey and, for a brief moment, they interact with the atoms that make you up. Then they continue on.

We spend a lot of time looking for the extraordinary—black holes, gravitational waves, possible biosignatures on distant exoplanets. Those things matter. But there’s something quietly astonishing about the ordinary: the fact that we can stand on a small rocky planet, look up, and literally be touched by light that predates stars, galaxies, and every living thing that has ever existed.

Curiosity doesn’t always need a destination. Sometimes it just needs a dark sky and the willingness to notice what’s already there.

That’s what I wanted to write about tonight. What about you?
